newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia pleased with economy -- minister.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia pleased with economy -- minister.

text.p: Yugoslavia will not downgrade its 1997 growth targets and will persist with its current economic policy despite missing the mark in the first half of the year, a senior government official said on Friday.
"The federal government firmly stands by the set economic targets and will not revise them for a single percent," said Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic.
"Our to date policy resulted in an industrial production rise, dynamic exports growth and improved living standard, accompanied by currency and prices stability," he said.

The government has also taken important steps towards privatisation. Through a partial sale of Telekom Srbija to foreign partners fresh funds were secured and were now reinvested in the country's basic industries like agriculture and export-oriented production, he told a news conference.
"This proves that our economic policy is correct and we will energetically persist on its further implementation," he added.
Yugoslavia predicted a 13 percent 1997 growth with exports rising 42 percent, imports 20, industrial production 13.9 and agriculture six percent.
But January-June year-on-year industrial output rose 7.6 percent with exports growing 28.5 percent and a trade gap exceeding $1 billion.
Statistics showed 0.1 percent month-on-month inflation in July, but 14.6 percent year-on-year level.

Analysts have criticised the government policy saying it failed to reach economic targets and businessmen blamed lack of foreign credits, shortage of working capital and insolvency for insufficient revival of production.
Sainovic admitted a slow realisation of the economic targets in the first quarter but said the general trends of current policy were positive.
After improved economic performance in the second quarter, Sainovic said it would be possible to achieve targeted growth by the year end.
"We expect speedier exports growth in the last two quarters due to late effects of the European Union perks and allocation of funds from the Serbian Development Fund," he said.
Analysts doubt the EU trade preferences granted to Yugoslavia at the end of April could lead to significant exports rise.
Outdated industry, after four years of isolation, simply cannot compete with price and quality on the world markets, they said.

Analysts also showed scepticism on effects of the credits extended by the Fund to export-oriented industries saying the money would be used for cash pay-outs instead of economically viable programmes.

"The only reason for the government decision to stick to its unrealistic targets is an oversized public spending. If they would downgrade the targets, they would also have to cut their spending. And that is what they do not want to do," the analyst said.
